metadata.title: Review, Not Repair.
metadata.subtitle: The Accessibility Review Skill
metadata.purpose: Take a Claude skill apart in the Teardown register: when Claude does an accessibility review, it isn't fixing the design — it's running a written list of steps in SKILL.md that check the design against WCAG 2.1 AA and report failures. Name the trade-off: they optimized for repeatability against a fixed standard at the expense of coverage beyond that standard and any repair of what it finds.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. You'd guess accessibility-review means Claude fixes the design. It doesn't — it checks the design against a fixed standard and reports where it fails. Here's what's actually happening.

beats.narration_text: Take a Claude skill apart, and here's what's inside. It's a folder — Claude reads it before it acts. This one's called accessibility-review. Open it up: one file, SKILL.md. About four kilobytes. Plain language, no hidden logic underneath. Claude reads the file, then acts on what it says. The file is the program.

Here's how it gets picked up. The file's description tells Claude exactly when to run it: auditing accessibility, checking a11y, asking whether a design is accessible — or before handing off work that touches color contrast, keyboard navigation, touch target size, or screen reader behavior. Words match, skill fires. Once triggered, Claude opens the Steps section and runs them top to bottom — linear, no branching unless a step says so.

production_viz.label: HOW IT GETS PICKED UP
production_viz.caption: only runs when the words match

beats.narration_text: That's an audit, not a repair — and that's a design choice. They optimized for two things: repeatability, and checking against a fixed, published standard. Run the same design through twice, and you get the same report both times. Here's what it costs. The skill won't rewrite the design to close the gaps it finds — it only reports them. And it only sees what WCAG 2.1 AA covers. Anything outside that standard is outside what this skill sees.

production_viz.label: AN AUDIT, NOT A REPAIR
production_viz.caption: it reports gaps, it doesn't close them

beats.narration_text: accessibility-review doesn't fix your design — it checks it against WCAG 2.1 AA and reports exactly where it fails, the same way every time. They optimized for a fixed standard; anything outside it, it's blind to.

props.quote: accessibility-review doesn't fix your design — it checks it against WCAG 2.1 AA and reports exactly where it fails, the same way every time. They optimized for a fixed standard; anything outside it, it's blind to.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: ask it to write a short SKILL.md for an accessibility-review skill, then run that skill on a design you describe. Watch it report failures against WCAG 2.1 AA without touching the design itself. Go deeper: run the same design through twice — do you get the same report? Then ask about something the standard doesn't cover, like cognitive load or reading level, and watch where the skill stops and the model starts guessing.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how a Claude 'skill' runs an accessibility audit. A Claude skill is a folder holding SKILL.md — a description telling Claude when to fire it, plus a numbered list of steps Claude reads and runs top to bottom, with no judgment step. Write me a short SKILL.md for an accessibility-review skill: a description that triggers on 'audit accessibility' / 'check a11y' / 'is this accessible?', plus three to five numbered steps that check a design's color contrast, keyboard navigation, and touch target size against WCAG 2.1 AA. Then run the skill on this design: white text (#FFFFFF) on light gray (#D4D4D4), 24-pixel-tall buttons, no visible focus ring, tap targets 32×32. Report each failure and the exact WCAG 2.1 AA criterion it violates. Do not fix the design — only report where it fails.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: run the same design through the skill twice — do you get the same report both times? Then ask about a case the standard doesn't cover, like cognitive load or reading level. Where does 'the standard' stop, and where does 'the model' start filling in?
